title: Maximizing the information obtained from chamber-based greenhouse gas exchange measurements in remote areas
author: Debouk, Altimir, et al.

steps.title: Assemble and power the system
steps.instruction: Connect the 12 V batteries to the 12 V–220 V converter, plug the laptop, and turn on the INNOVA 1412 PAS analyzer. Verify that the external air filter, the small fan (battery powered), and the AMPROBE TMD‑56 thermocouple logger are all powered.

steps.title: Install soil collars
steps.instruction: Place a metal collar (height = 8 cm, Ø = 25 cm) 3 cm deep in the soil at each sampling point and leave it in place for 2–3 weeks before any chamber measurements to minimise disturbance.

steps.title: Connect chamber and tubing
steps.instruction: Fit the transparent methacrylate chamber (nominal volume = 20 L, h = 38.5 cm, Ø = 25 cm) onto the rubber joint at the base of the collar. Attach the 20‑m Teflon sampling tube, the external air filter, the thermocouple (TMD‑56) and the fan. Ensure the PAS analyzer will draw air at 1 L min⁻¹ intermittently; the flow rate is generated by the analyzer itself, so no pump is needed.

steps.title: Ventilate chamber and record ambient gases
steps.instruction: Open the chamber for 4 min to allow complete ventilation of the headspace and to obtain ambient concentrations of CO₂, CH₄, N₂O and water vapor. Log these ambient values with the laptop.

steps.title: Measure flux under light
steps.instruction: Close the chamber around the collar for exactly 4 min (240 s) while the vegetation remains intact and natural sunlight reaches the chamber. The PAS cycle (≈ 60 s total, including flushing and sampling) will provide one concentration value per minute. Note that temperature inside the chamber typically rises 2–3 °C (up to 5 °C on hot days) and that <10 s are required to remove ≈ 1 % of the headspace air; >50 s remain for air replacement before the next sample.

steps.title: Measure flux under dark
steps.instruction: Cover the chamber with the reflective dark cover and repeat the 4‑min closure exactly as above, recording the same gas concentrations under dark conditions.

steps.title: Measure soil‑only flux
steps.instruction: Cut all above‑ground vegetation within the chamber, then close the dark‑covered chamber for another 4 min and record the gas concentrations. This yields soil‑only fluxes.

steps.title: Calculate fluxes from concentration data
steps.instruction: For each 4‑min closure compute the linear slope of concentration versus time (ΔC/Δt) and multiply by the chamber volume (V = 0.020 m³) to obtain flux: F = V · ΔC/Δt (mol s⁻¹). Positive values indicate emission, negative values uptake.

steps.title: Correct CH₄ for water‑vapor interference
steps.instruction: If the measured water‑vapor concentration exceeds 12 mol m⁻³, adjust the CH₄ value by subtracting 1.104 × ΔH₂O (where ΔH₂O is the change in water‑vapor concentration since the previous measurement).

steps.title: Determine detection limits and fit quality
steps.instruction: Calculate the detection limit (DL) for each gas as DL = V × SD_A × t, where SD_A is the standard deviation of the ambient concentration series and t = 240 s. Assess the linear fit by its r²; consider the fit good if r² > 0.2.

steps.title: Assign quality flags and discard unreliable data
steps.instruction: Use the following flag scheme: Flag 0 – no water‑vapor correction, r² > 0.2, flux > DL; Flag 1 – correction applied, r² > 0.2, flux > DL; Flag 2 – correction applied, r² > 0.2, flux ≤ DL; Flag 3 – no correction, r² ≤ 0.2, flux ≤ DL. Discard all measurements with Flag 3. Note that the PAS detection limits are 5 ppm (CO₂), 0.03 ppm (N₂O) and 0.24 ppm (CH₄); in this study 37 % of N₂O and 47 % of CH₄ measurements fell below their respective DLs.
